bib.title: 2. Controlling Content Style (Generative AI Design Patterns)
bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly), authorship and year inferred from filename and in-text dates June/July 2025; not printed in the PDF text

question: How can an application control the style, format and content constraints of foundation-model output more robustly than prompt engineering?
contributions: Five patterns: Logits Masking, Grammar, Style Transfer, Reverse Neutralization, Content Optimization

results.claim: Try-and-try-again is acceptable only when failure rate is under about 10 percent.
results.setup: Regenerating LLM output until it passes style rules
results.quote: only works for edge cases when very few responses (less than 10% or so) need to be regenerated

results.claim: With 10% failure, expected attempts are about 1.1 and mean latency rises 10%.

limits: Examples are single anecdotal outputs with no repeated runs, metrics or baselines.
Logits Masking requires logit access; Claude lacks it (June 2025) and per-token client round trips add latency, so mostly local models.
Grammar can cause endless whitespace, increased refusals on nested or long structures, and inaccurate results when too restrictive.
Style Transfer by few-shot or fine-tuning gives only implicit enforcement.
Content Optimization depends entirely on evaluator quality and the in-distribution requirement; gaming of metrics is possible.
Provider support statements are dated June/July 2025 and may have changed; the Claude footnote says it used prefilling, not constrained decoding, as of July 2025.
practices: Use Logits Masking (zero logits of rule-violating continuations, set to -inf) when rules are dynamic, logic-based, fetched from a database or depend on user input (Pattern 1, Pattern 2 Alternatives).
Do not rely on try-and-try-again unless the success rate is very high; latency grows as 100/p and tail latency is unbounded (Pattern 1 sidebar).
For format constraints prefer provider-side structured outputs (Pydantic or dataclass schema) over BNF unless rules go beyond data format or logprobs are available (Pattern 2 Variations).
State JSON explicitly in the prompt even when using JSON mode (Pattern 2 Option 2).
Do not beg for compliance in the prompt; use Grammar, e.g. Literal["YES","NO"] (Pattern 2 sidebar).
Give a restrictive grammar an escape value such as Literal["Unknown"] (Pattern 2 Caveats).
Check that structured-output support is real constrained decoding rather than an extra post-processing LLM call (Pattern 2 Caveats).
Use few-shot examples (1 to 10) first; move to fine-tuning for higher fidelity, shorter prompts and cheaper inference (Pattern 3).
Use standardized placeholders such as {name} and {deadline} so downstream code can substitute values (Pattern 3 Problem).
For image style transfer add a depth-map control image to preserve spatial layout (Pattern 3 images).
Choose a repeatable neutral form and check neutralization with embedding cosine similarity, avoiding over-neutralization (Pattern 4 Considerations).
Cover the topic range of inputs and outputs in the fine-tuning set, using topic modeling (Pattern 4 Dataset considerations).
Build preference pairs by repeated generation, changed settings or prompt rewriting; the latter two cover more style space (Pattern 5).
Invest most effort in the evaluation step; avoid narrow proxy metrics and separate metric from true objective (Pattern 5 Evaluation matters).
Use DPO rather than RL for preference tuning; quality of preference data trumps quantity; iterate until saturation (Pattern 5).
Satisfy the in-distribution requirement by using the same LLM to generate and tune, or SFT first (Pattern 5).
